title: Federal duplication and fragmentation remain a public-capacity problem even after large realized savings
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office 16th annual duplication, overlap, and fragmentation review
geography: United States federal programs and agencies; matters for congressional and administrative action

observations.period: May 2026; federal duplication, overlap, and fragmentation portfolio

denominator.unit: remaining matters and recommendations identified by GAO for congressional or agency consideration

new_matters.unit: new matters and recommendations identified in the 2026 annual report

realized_savings.unit: billion dollars in reported cumulative cost savings and revenue increases from congressional and agency action

future_potential.unit: billion dollars in potential additional savings or revenue increases if remaining suggestions are addressed

capacity_consequence.value: remaining duplication, overlap, and fragmentation can reduce efficiency and effectiveness and complicate service delivery and oversight

observations.method: GAO annual cross-government review of prior recommendations and new matters involving duplicative, overlapping, or fragmented federal programs, goals, or actions.
observations.uncertainty: Reported savings and potential are GAO portfolio estimates and do not identify household incidence, implementation cost, service quality, or whether every remaining matter is politically or administratively feasible.
observations.subgroup: Federal agencies, Congress, state and local implementers, firms receiving or complying with federal programs, and households relying on public services or transfers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some overlap can provide redundancy, specialization, or access points; eliminating programs may create transition costs or remove valuable local, sector-specific, or resilience capacity.

related_sources.claim: Full GAO annual report on duplication, overlap, and fragmentation.

boundary: This record measures a GAO portfolio of federal duplication, overlap, and fragmentation matters and reported fiscal potential. It does not establish a national service-failure rate, household savings, agency productivity, public trust, or the causal effect of consolidating any program.
